method: Checked canonical headings and opening text at SriGranth; genre and performance context checked against the Sikh Research Institute Guru Granth Sahib Project; matched exact BaniDB provider data supplied by root. Summaries paraphrase the opening content rather than claiming an exhaustive interpretation.

entries.displayName: Seven Days in Gauri (Bhagat Kabir Ji)
entries.context: Bhagat Kabir Ji uses the seven weekdays to encourage daily praise and remembrance of the Divine in this Gauri composition.
entries.claimSupport: The heading explicitly identifies seven weekdays. Preserve this exact reading; it is not an additional ballad Vaar.

entries.displayName: Seven Days in Bilaval (Guru Amar Das Ji)
entries.context: Guru Amar Das Ji uses the weekdays as a framework for remembering the Divine presence and finding peace through the Name.
entries.claimSupport: Provider selection ends at the first ten-stanza sequence (10|1) on Ang 842; do not conflate it with the following Bilaval sequence or the Fourth Guru Vaar.

entries.context: Guru Ram Das Ji’s Sri Raag Vaar opens with saloks connecting love of truth with reflection on the Guru’s word.
entries.claimSupport: Vaar heading: Fourth Guru; opening saloks: Third Guru.

entries.context: Guru Nanak Dev Ji’s Majh Vaar opens by praising the Guru as a source of light and peace, then examines changing human attachments.
entries.claimSupport: Heading identifies First Guru and the Malik Murid/Chandrahara Sohiya tune.

entries.context: Guru Ram Das Ji’s Gauri Vaar opens with the True Guru’s equal regard for everyone and the importance of sincere devotion.
entries.claimSupport: Fourth Guru Gauri Vaar, distinct from ID89.

entries.context: Guru Arjan Dev Ji’s Gauri Vaar opens with remembrance of the Divine Name and spiritual company as support through suffering.
entries.claimSupport: Fifth Guru Gauri Vaar, distinct from ID88.

entries.context: Guru Nanak Dev Ji’s Asa Vaar joins pauris and saloks in reflection on the Guru’s guidance and the Divine present throughout creation.
entries.authorship: Guru Nanak Dev Ji (Vaar); Guru Angad Dev Ji (some saloks); Guru Ram Das Ji (accompanying chhants)
entries.claimSupport: Actual provider sequence begins with Fourth Guru chhants on Ang 448 and interleaves Ang448–451 material with the Vaar on Ang462–475; preserve that sequence.

entries.context: Guru Amar Das Ji’s Gujari Vaar contrasts possessive attachment with a life guided by the Guru and remembrance of the Divine.
entries.claimSupport: Third Guru Gujari Vaar, distinct from ID92.

entries.context: Guru Arjan Dev Ji’s Gujari Vaar opens with a call to remember the Guru inwardly, in speech, in seeing and in listening.
entries.claimSupport: Fifth Guru Gujari Vaar, distinct from ID91.

entries.context: Guru Ram Das Ji’s Bihagara Vaar opens with saloks on finding peace through serving the Guru and receiving the Divine Name.
entries.claimSupport: Fourth Guru Vaar; opening saloks belong to Third Guru.

entries.context: Guru Ram Das Ji’s Vadhans Vaar opens with saloks that use swan imagery for those absorbed in the Guru’s word and the True Name.
entries.claimSupport: Fourth Guru Vaar; opening saloks belong to Third Guru.

entries.context: Guru Ram Das Ji’s Sorath Vaar opens with the image of a devoted bride to explore inner truth and love of the Divine.
entries.claimSupport: Fourth Guru Vaar; opening salok belongs to First Guru.

entries.context: Guru Arjan Dev Ji’s Jaitsri Vaar opens by affirming the Divine presence through all time and the value of remembrance.
entries.claimSupport: Heading explicitly states Fifth Guru and Vaar with saloks.

entries.context: Guru Amar Das Ji’s Suhi Vaar opens with bride imagery that contrasts devotion to the Divine with attachment and divided love.
entries.claimSupport: Heading identifies Third Guru and Vaar with saloks.

entries.context: Guru Ram Das Ji’s Bilaval Vaar begins with praise and attention to the Guru’s teaching, picturing the renewed mind as a flourishing garden.
entries.claimSupport: Fourth Guru ballad Vaar; not the Seven Days work ID51.

entries.context: Guru Amar Das Ji’s Ramkali Vaar opens with a field-and-seed image of the Guru’s wisdom, the Divine Name and freedom from ego.
entries.claimSupport: Third Guru Ramkali Vaar, distinct from IDs100/101.

entries.context: Guru Arjan Dev Ji’s Ramkali Vaar opens by praising the Guru’s role in overcoming ego and reuniting the separated with the Divine.
entries.claimSupport: Fifth Guru Ramkali Vaar, distinct from IDs99/101.

entries.context: Satta and Balvand’s Ramkali Vaar celebrates the continuity of Guruship from Guru Nanak Dev Ji through Guru Arjan Dev Ji.
entries.claimSupport: Heading names both Balvand and Satta; Ang967 honours Mata Khivi and langar, Ang968 explicitly honours Guru Arjan.

entries.context: Guru Amar Das Ji’s Maru Vaar opens with a salok that uses buying and selling to explore the recognition and worth of virtue.
entries.claimSupport: Third Guru Maru Vaar, with First Guru opening salok; distinct from ID103.

entries.context: Guru Arjan Dev Ji’s Maru Vaar pairs pauris with dakhane verses, beginning with devotion and longing for the Divine beloved.
entries.claimSupport: Heading names Fifth Guru and dakhane; distinct from ID102.

entries.context: Guru Arjan Dev Ji’s brief Basant Vaar uses spring and blossoming as images of renewal through the Divine Name and spiritual company.
entries.claimSupport: Fifth Guru; primary text uses spring/green growth images.

entries.context: Guru Ram Das Ji’s Sarang Vaar opens with saloks portraying the Guru as the key that unlocks attachment within the mind.
entries.claimSupport: Fourth Guru Vaar; first salok belongs to Second Guru.

entries.context: Guru Nanak Dev Ji’s Malhar Vaar opens with a salok likening the joy of meeting the Guru to rain reviving the earth.
entries.claimSupport: First Guru Vaar; opening salok belongs to Third Guru.

entries.context: Guru Ram Das Ji’s Kanara Vaar opens with a call to hold the Divine Name in the heart, practise humility and overcome ego.
entries.claimSupport: Primary heading is Fourth Guru, not Fifth Guru; preceding Ang1312 chhant has a separate Fifth Guru heading.
